Family Health

Can a Pap test hurt? Making cervical screening more comfortable

Updated: October 5, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A Pap test is usually brief, but it does not feel the same for everyone. Some people notice pressure, a scraping sensation or mild discomfort; others find the examination painful. A first appointment can feel unfamiliar, but pain should not be dismissed as inexperience or a low pain threshold. You can ask for adjustments, pause or stop at any stage. Understanding the purpose and steps can help you plan an appointment that feels more manageable.

What a Pap test checks: and what an HPV test checks

A Pap test, also called a Pap smear or cervical cytology, examines cells collected from the cervix, the opening between the vagina and womb. It looks for changes that may need monitoring or treatment before they progress to cervical cancer.

An HPV test looks for high-risk types of human papillomavirus. Persistent infection with certain HPV types causes most cervical cancers. Programmes may use HPV testing first, a Pap test alone or both together, called co-testing. The sample collection can look similar even though the laboratory tests differ.

Finding an abnormality does not automatically mean cancer. Further testing helps establish its significance. Screening is intended to prevent cervical cancer; it is not a general check for every reproductive condition, other gynaecological cancers or all sexually transmitted infections.

Who should have cervical screening?

Screening is offered to eligible people who have a cervix. Starting age, intervals and stopping rules depend on the local programme and personal history. It is not correct to say that everyone needs a Pap test, or that being sexually active automatically means screening should start before the programme’s recommended age.

HPV can pass through intimate skin-to-skin sexual contact, including contact without vaginal intercourse. Not currently having sex does not necessarily remove the need for screening, because an earlier infection can persist or become detectable later. If you have never had sexual contact, discuss your circumstances rather than assuming that one rule applies in every country.

Menopause does not automatically end screening. Neither does HPV vaccination remove every reason for screening. The relevant question is whether you meet your programme’s eligibility and stopping criteria.

After a hysterectomy, ask whether the cervix was removed. If it remains, screening may still be needed. If it was removed, the reason for surgery and any history of high-grade cell changes or cancer determine whether further surveillance is required. Do not continue or stop solely because the operation was called a hysterectomy.

How often is screening needed?

Intervals are based on the type of test, previous results and risk. Repeating a Pap test every year is not the routine schedule for most average-risk people, and testing more often is not automatically more helpful.

For example, US ACOG guidance retains cervical cytology every three years for average-risk people aged 21–29. Its 2026 update prefers primary high-risk HPV testing every five years for ages 30–65 and includes a patient-collected HPV option every three years with appropriate follow-up systems. Your clinician can explain which available test fits your circumstances.

British Columbia uses a different programme: screening generally begins at 25, with HPV screening every five years or cytology every three years, depending on availability and prior history. Stopping at 69 requires the programme’s negative-result and history criteria. These are regional examples, not instructions to choose whichever interval is longest.

HIV, other causes of immune suppression, previous high-grade abnormalities or treatment can require closer surveillance. An abnormal result may also change the next date. Keep the schedule provided by your screening service rather than using a general age table to override it.

A pelvic examination is a separate assessment

A pelvic examination can include looking at the vulva and vaginal opening for redness, irritation, unusual discharge or other changes. A speculum may be used to view the vagina and cervix. A Pap or HPV sample can be taken during that examination if due, but the examination itself is not the screening test.

Sometimes a clinician recommends a bimanual examination: one or two gloved fingers are placed in the vagina while the other hand presses gently on the lower abdomen. This can help assess tenderness or the size and position of pelvic structures. It does not directly show the ovaries or reliably rule out all ovarian or uterine disease.

Not everyone needs a full pelvic examination every year. Symptoms, medical history and the purpose of the visit guide the decision. Most contraceptive prescriptions do not require one; fitting certain devices, such as an IUD or diaphragm, is a different situation.

Ask which parts are proposed and why. Agreeing to cervical sampling does not automatically mean agreeing to every other examination.

Can you attend during a period?

Blood can make a cervical cell sample harder to assess, so routine screening is usually best booked outside a period. Light spotting does not always prevent sampling, but contact the clinic if you are bleeding on the appointment day; the answer can depend on the test and programme.

If periods are irregular or frequent, ask the service to help arrange a workable plan rather than postponing repeatedly. Bleeding after sex, between periods or after menopause needs assessment in its own right. Do not delay that assessment while waiting for a day suitable for routine screening.

Tell the clinic if you are or may be pregnant, have recently given birth or have had cervical or uterine treatment. Routine screening and follow-up after an abnormal result may have different timing requirements.

Before the appointment: preparation and practical support

Ask for the clinic’s preparation instructions. For clinician-collected screening, programmes often advise avoiding vaginal medicines, creams and lubricants for about two days beforehand; advice about intercourse and tampons can vary. Do not stop prescribed treatment without checking, and tell the sample-taker what you have used.

Avoid douching. If you are being treated for unusual discharge or a pelvic infection, ask when screening should be scheduled. Treatment prescribed specifically to make sampling more comfortable, such as a course for vaginal dryness, needs its own timing plan.

You can ask for a longer appointment, an examiner you feel comfortable with, an interpreter, a chaperone or a trusted person to accompany you. A friend, partner or relative can provide support without speaking for you or making decisions about consent.

If a full bladder makes pelvic pressure uncomfortable, ask to use the toilet first. Check whether the clinic needs a urine sample before emptying your bladder. A skirt or long top may help you feel covered, and the clinic should provide privacy and a sheet or gown.

What happens during the sample collection?

A trained nurse, doctor, midwife or other qualified sample-taker will confirm your details and relevant health history, explain the test and obtain your consent. Tell them if this is your first test or if you want more time for questions.

You undress privately from the waist down and lie in a suitable position. Commonly this means lying on your back with knees bent and apart; some clinics use foot supports. A side-lying position may be possible if that is more comfortable.

The clinician gently inserts a speculum into the vagina. This hinged plastic or metal instrument opens enough to make the cervix visible. A light helps the clinician see, and an appropriate small amount of lubricant may be used according to sampling guidance.

A soft brush collects cells from the cervix. The speculum is then closed and removed, and you can get dressed. The sampling part is usually only a few minutes. NHS guidance describes the test as generally under five minutes and the appointment around ten, but extra time for comfort or discussion is appropriate.

Ways to reduce discomfort during the test

Ask about an appropriately sized speculum. A smaller one may help, although the examiner also needs to be able to see the cervix. If cold metal is unpleasant, ask whether a plastic or suitably warmed instrument is available.

You may prefer to hear each step before it happens, or you may want less commentary. You can bring music or another calming distraction while keeping a way to communicate with the clinician. Agree a simple stop signal before the examination begins.

Slow breathing and relaxing the pelvic floor may reduce involuntary bracing, but they are options rather than a test of how well you can tolerate pain. Ask about changing position, a pause or inserting the speculum yourself initially if the clinic offers that approach.

Speak up as soon as something hurts; you do not have to wait until it is unbearable. The clinician can stop and discuss another approach or appointment. Being unable to complete the test that day is not a failure.

Pain relief and vaginal dryness need an individual plan

If you have had painful sampling, discuss this before the next appointment. Ask whether an over-the-counter pain medicine would be appropriate for you and when to take it. Do not assume ibuprofen is suitable, particularly if you may be pregnant, have certain health conditions or take medicines that interact with it.

Oral pain relief does not reliably solve pain caused by a speculum, muscle tightening or trauma. Treatment for significant dryness, sometimes including prescribed vaginal estrogen when appropriate, may be more useful than trying to push through an uncomfortable examination.

Do not apply numbing cream or another vaginal product on your own immediately before sampling. Discuss suitable options and their timing with the clinician and laboratory requirements. The blanket claim that no pain-management option is possible because it always invalidates a Pap test is not a useful rule.

IUD insertion, cervical biopsy and routine screening are different procedures. The pain-relief plan used for one should not be assumed to apply unchanged to another.

Conditions and experiences that can make screening harder

Vaginal dryness can make insertion uncomfortable. Vaginismus involves involuntary tightening around penetration. Vulvodynia is persistent vulval pain and does not necessarily involve visible inflammation. Endometriosis, in which tissue similar to the womb lining grows elsewhere, can also contribute to pelvic pain.

Tell the clinician about diagnosed conditions or symptoms even if you do not yet have a diagnosis. The goal is to adapt care, not to make you prove a reason for pain.

Not having had vaginal intercourse does not guarantee that screening will hurt, just as having had intercourse does not guarantee comfort. Anatomy, muscle response, dryness, expectations and the approach to the examination all vary. You can request adjustments regardless of your sexual history.

Previous sexual trauma or distressing medical experiences may make screening difficult. You do not need to recount the details to ask for trauma-informed care. A trusted examiner, explicit permission before each step, a support person and control over stopping can be part of the plan.

Could self-collected HPV testing be an option?

Some programmes offer eligible people a self-collected vaginal sample for HPV testing. This may help when a speculum examination is a barrier, but access, approved kits and follow-up pathways differ by region.

It is an HPV test, not a self-administered Pap test. Depending on the result, you may still need clinician-collected cells, a speculum examination or colposcopy. Ask which option is available and what happens after a positive result.

Symptoms such as unexplained bleeding or persistent unusual discharge need clinical assessment even if self-sampling is available or a recent screening result was reassuring.

Spotting and cramps after the appointment

Some people have a small amount of spotting after the cervix is brushed. Others have none. A liner or pad may be useful. Brief mild cramps can also occur, but significant pain should not be treated as an expected requirement of screening.

If you feel mildly crampy, a comfortably warm, wrapped heat pack may help. Ask about a pain medicine that is safe for you if needed. Avoid excessive heat or relying on home measures for worsening symptoms.

NHS advice says light spotting should stop within a few hours and recommends contacting a clinician if it continues or if bleeding is heavy. Follow any specific aftercare instructions you receive. Do not wait three days to ask for help if symptoms are concerning.

Seek prompt advice for significant or increasing pelvic pain, fever, heavy bleeding or persistent bleeding. Heavy bleeding with faintness, collapse or severe pain needs urgent emergency assessment. If a biopsy or treatment was also performed, its aftercare may differ from a simple screening sample.

Getting and understanding the result

Ask when and how the result will arrive. Turnaround depends on the laboratory and programme; a week is not a reliable promise everywhere. Contact the service if the result is overdue, and do not assume that no message means everything was normal.

A normal or negative Pap result means no abnormal cells were identified in that sample. An HPV-negative result means high-risk HPV was not detected. Neither replaces assessment of new symptoms or overrides a personalised surveillance plan.

An unsatisfactory sample means the laboratory could not assess it adequately, for example because too few cells were collected or blood obscured them. This is different from an abnormal-cell result. The service should give you a date for repeat sampling.

An abnormal Pap result means some cells look different; it does not automatically mean precancer or cancer. Irritation, some infections and hormonal changes can affect cell appearance, while HPV-related changes have their own follow-up pathways. An HPV-positive result is also not itself a cancer diagnosis.

When further tests or treatment are recommended

The next step depends on the exact result and previous history. It may be another HPV or Pap test, a shorter follow-up interval or colposcopy. If infection is suspected, separate testing may be appropriate. A Pap test should not be used as a dependable test for thrush, herpes, trichomoniasis or all other infections.

Colposcopy uses magnification to examine the cervix more closely. A speculum is used, but the viewing instrument stays outside the body. A small biopsy may be taken for laboratory examination if needed; a Pap test alone does not establish every cancer diagnosis.

If high-grade changes are found, the team may discuss removing or treating abnormal tissue to reduce future cancer risk. Not every abnormal result needs immediate treatment. Ask what your result means, the reason for the recommended follow-up and whom to contact if the appointment does not arrive.

A useful appointment respects both prevention and comfort

Cervical screening can prevent cancer by identifying risk or cell changes early. It works best when eligible people can attend, receive their results and complete the follow-up that is recommended.

Comfort and consent are part of that process. Tell the service what would help, ask for a different clinician if needed and make a plan for pain or distress rather than abandoning care or forcing yourself through an examination. Screening should fit an informed decision about your health.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

NHS guidance describes a brief clinician-collected sample, practical adjustments and the right to stop. Persistent bleeding or significant pain after screening warrants advice rather than being dismissed as routine.

ACOG and BC Cancer guidance illustrate why test type, age, history and location determine the screening schedule. NCI guidance distinguishes HPV results, cell abnormalities and inadequate samples, with follow-up based on the specific findings.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you prepare questions about the test, comfort measures and follow-up. Bring your screening history and explain what support you want. This article cannot determine your eligibility or replace your local programme’s instructions.

When to seek help

Ask to pause or stop if the examination is painful or distressing. Contact the clinic for heavy or persistent bleeding, worsening pain or fever afterward. Bleeding after sex or menopause and other unexplained symptoms need assessment even after a normal screening result.

Evidence notes updated: October 5, 2026

Key takeaways

  • A Pap test, an HPV test and a pelvic examination are different.
  • Screening schedules depend on your programme and medical history.
  • Pain deserves adjustments; you can stop at any point.
  • Tell the clinic about dryness, pelvic pain, pregnancy or previous difficult examinations.
  • An inadequate sample is different from an abnormal-cell result.
  • Make sure you receive the result and understand the next step.

Frequently asked questions

Does a first Pap test have to hurt?

No. Experiences vary, and pain should not be dismissed as lack of experience. Ask for a pause, a different approach or a plan for another appointment.

Do I need screening if I am not currently having sex?

You may, because previous HPV exposure can remain relevant. Your age, screening history and local programme determine the recommendation.

Do I need a Pap test every year?

Most average-risk people do not. Intervals depend on whether the programme uses HPV testing, cytology or both and on previous results.

Can I have screening while on my period?

Contact the clinic. Routine sampling is usually best outside a period, although light spotting may not always prevent it. Unexplained bleeding needs separate assessment.

Can I bring someone or ask for a smaller speculum?

Yes, ask when booking. A support person, appropriately sized speculum, another position or a longer appointment may make the visit easier.

Is self-sampling the same as doing a Pap test at home?

No. Approved self-sampling generally tests a vaginal sample for HPV. It does not examine cervical cells like a Pap test, and further clinician assessment may be needed.

Is bleeding for several days normal after a simple sample?

Do not assume so. Small amounts of spotting usually settle quickly. Contact the service if spotting persists or bleeding is heavy, and seek urgent help for severe symptoms.

Does an abnormal result mean cancer?

Usually it does not. The precise HPV or cell result and your history determine whether repeat testing, colposcopy or treatment is recommended.

Can a normal screening result explain away symptoms?

No. Unexplained bleeding, unusual discharge or persistent pelvic pain should be assessed even if screening was recently normal.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
